docs.title: Home
docs.text:
🐝hiveBr🐝 is a lightweight 2D simulation framework for single- and multi-robot mobile navigation. It ships a Pygame-based physics/renderer engine and a clean OpenLab API that lets the same user script run a fleet locally or on a physical arena.

Robots in the simulator are called B-bots (for bee), keeping with the hive metaphor.

docs.title: Why hiveBr?
docs.text:
• Mono or fleet, one API. A single robot is just a fleet with N = 1.
  • Dual paradigm. Write decentralized logic with HiveBrAgent (one instance per B-bot) or centralized logic with SwarmController (one object for the whole fleet).
  • Interactive GUI. Pan, zoom, load occupancy-grid maps, switch themes, toggle LiDAR, and add waypoints/obstacles with the mouse.
  • Two environment representations. Analytic circular obstacles and image-based occupancy grids with inflation.
  • Precision sensing. Ray-casting LiDAR using a DDA algorithm against the grid plus analytic circle intersections.
  • Deterministic fleets. Every timestep is computed from a frozen snapshot of the fleet state, so results are independent of robot update order.
  • Research-ready. Pluggable controllers, path planners (A, RRT, RRT, PRM, BIT*, OMPL, RRT-Dubins), and a data logger for offline analysis.

docs.title: A 20-second taste
docs.text:
from hivebr import HiveBrAgent, SwarmExperiment

class Patrol(HiveBrAgent):
    def loop(self, state, neighbors):
        # state.goal holds the current waypoint (x, y, theta)
        return 0.5, 0.0

exp = SwarmExperiment(robots=3, backend="navsim2d")
exp.assign_agent(robot_ids=[0, 1, 2], agent_class=Patrol)
exp.assign_route(0, [[5, 2, 0.0], [5, 6, 0.0]])
exp.run()

Switching backend="ros2" reuses the same agent code on the physical lab.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: A configuration is a plain dictionary. The engine ships with a default (hivebr.engine.simulator.DEFAULT_CONFIG) and examples usually load config/default.yaml with load_config.

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
window:
  width: 1400
  height: 750
  min_width: 1100
  min_height: 650
  panel_width: 300
  title: "hivebr"

world:
  width: 20.0
  height: 12.0
  grid_size: 1.0
  obstacle_radius: 0.4
  show_origin: true
  show_axes: true
  show_inflation: true
  # map_image: "maze.png"     # optional occupancy-grid map
  # resolution: 0.1           # metres per pixel
  recharge_places:
    - [3, 3]
    - [5, 5]

camera:
  initial_zoom: 1.0
  min_zoom: 0.25
  max_zoom: 8.0
  zoom_step: 1.1
  margin_x: 1.0
  margin_y: 1.0

# Default B-bot (used directly for N = 1, and as base for the fleet)
robot:
  type: differential
  initial_pose: [2.5, 2.5, 0.0]
  radius: 0.1375
  length: 0.39
  width: 0.275
  wheel_base: 0.285
  max_speed: 3.0
  max_omega: 4.0
  max_steer: 0.52
  tau_v: 0.2                 # first-order motor time constant
  path_max_length: 4000

# Optional fleet: each entry overrides `robot` and may carry a color
robots:
  - { id: 0, type: differential, initial_pose: [2.0, 2.0, 0.0], radius: 0.25 }
  - { id: 1, type: differential, initial_pose: [5.0, 5.0, 0.0], radius: 0.25,
      color: [220, 20, 60] }

lidar:
  enabled: false
  num_rays: 101
  range: 12.0
  fov_deg: 360

# Gaussian actuation noise on the commanded velocities
noise:
  enabled: false
  sigma_v: 0.0               # std of the linear velocity error (m/s)
  sigma_omega: 0.0           # std of the angular velocity error (rad/s)
  limit: 3.0                 # truncate the error at +/- limit * sigma
  seed: null                 # optional RNG seed for reproducibility

waypoints:
  goal_tolerance: 0.5
  define_orientation: true
  show_tolerance_circle: false
  points: []                 # global list, applied to B-bot 0

interaction:
  collision_policy: stop     # "stop" | "resolve" | "none"
  robot_collision: true      # master switch for robot-robot collision checks
  robot_safety_margin: 0.0
  resolve_push: 0.05
  comm_radius: null          # null = full visibility
  show_robot_links: false

show_times: true             # HUD per-B-bot timing (line followers)

obstacles:
  - { x: 6.0, y: 5.0, radius: 1.2 }

colors:
  background: [30, 30, 30]
  robot: [30, 144, 255]
  fleet:
    - [30, 144, 255]
    - [220, 20, 60]
    - [50, 205, 50]
    - [255, 165, 0]
    - [148, 0, 211]
    - [0, 206, 209]
    - [255, 105, 180]
    - [255, 215, 0]

theme: dark                  # "dark" | "light"

docs.title: Section reference
docs.text: Section Key Meaning window width, height Initial window size in pixels. min_width, min_height Lower bound when resizing. panel_width Width of the right control panel. world width, height World size in metres. grid_size Background grid spacing. obstacle_radius Default radius for mouse-added obstacles. map_image, resolution Occupancy-grid source image and metres/pixel. line_map_image Line-follower track image (black line on white), rendered as background. recharge_places Charging spots ([x, y] or [x, y, r]). camera initial_zoom, min_zoom, max_zoom Zoom limits. robot type Kinematic model (see Robot Models). initial_pose [x, y, theta] spawn pose. radius Collision radius (for differential/ackermann/boat). For hexagonal_holonomic: distance from center to wheel center L (m). wheel_radius (hexagonal_holonomic) Wheel radius r (m). max_wheel_speed (hexagonal_holonomic) Max wheel angular velocity (rad/s). max_speed, max_omega, max_steer Actuation limits. tau_v First-order velocity time constant. servo_max_speed (hexagonal_holonomic) Max servo speed for control allocation (rad/s). num_sensors, line_width, sensor_offset, sensor_span, sensor_aperture, sensor_noise, line_threshold Line-follower TCRT5000 array. lap_detection_radius, min_lap_distance, min_lap_time, lost_timeout Line-follower lap timing / end-of-track detection. robots list of specs Fleet; each overrides robot and may set color. lidar enabled, num_rays, range, fov_deg Sensor settings. noise enabled Inject Gaussian noise on the actuated velocities. sigma_v, sigma_omega Std of the linear / angular velocity error. sigma Alias applied to both sigma_v and sigma_omega. limit Truncate the sampled error at +/- limit * sigma. seed Optional RNG seed (reproducible runs). waypoints goal_tolerance Distance to consider a waypoint reached. define_orientation Ask for a final heading when adding waypoints. interaction collision_policy stop, resolve or none for B-bot pairs. robot_collision Master switch; false disables robot-robot collision checks entirely. robot_safety_margin Extra separation added to r_i + r_j. comm_radius Visibility radius for decentralized neighbors. show_robot_links Draw communication links between neighbors. show_times Show per-B-bot timing in the HUD (toggled by Toggle Times). theme dark or light palette. gui buttons List of sidebar buttons to show (see below). sliders List of sidebar sliders to show (see below).

docs.text:
Control which parameter sliders appear in the right sidebar. Default shows common sliders.

Key Slider Config Path Range Applies To max_speed Max Speed robot.max_speed 0.2 – 8.0 All except line_follower max_omega Max Omega robot.max_omega 0.1 – 6.0 All except line_follower max_steer Max Steering robot.max_steer 0.1 – 1.2 Ackermann grid_size Grid Size world.grid_size 0.1 – 5.0 All noise_sigma Noise Sigma noise.sigma_v, noise.sigma_omega 0.0 – 1.0 All servo_max_speed Max Servo Speed robot.servo_max_speed 0.5 – 30.0 Hexagonal Holonomic

Example:

    - max_speed
    - max_omega
    - grid_size
    - noise_sigma

Mono is fleet with N = 1

If robots is omitted, the engine builds a single B-bot from robot. Adding robots is the only change needed to go multi-robot.

docs.title: Controllers
docs.text:
A controller maps the current situation to a velocity command. In the low-level engine it is any callable with this signature:

def controller(robot, world, goal, config, dt, lidar_readings=None) -> dict:
    ...
  • robot — the B-bot being controlled (has .x, .y, .theta, .position, .max_speed, .max_omega, …).
  • world — the environment (.obstacles, .grid_map, .recharge_places).
  • goal — the current waypoint [x, y, theta] or None.
  • config — the full configuration dictionary.
  • dt — timestep in seconds.
  • lidar_readings — list of (angle, distance, hit) tuples.

The engine also accepts 5-argument controllers (without lidar_readings) and falls back automatically.

High-level API

With HiveBrAgent you implement loop(state, neighbors) instead, where the goal arrives inside state.goal. See the OpenLab API.

docs.title: Controllers shipped in examples/controllers
docs.text: Controller Import Idea potential_field_controller examples.controllers.potential_field Artificial potential fields with collision-recovery FSM, local-minima detection, virtual subgoals and tangential repulsion. potential_field_controller examples.controllers.potential_field2 Lighter potential-field variant. vortex_apf_controller examples.controllers.vortex_apf Vortex artificial potential fields — circulating flux around obstacles to avoid local minima. waypoint_follower_controller examples.controllers.waypoint_follower_controller Pure pursuit / heading tracking to the current waypoint. simple_ackermann_controller examples.controllers.simple_ackermann_controller Steering controller for Ackermann B-bots. PlannerController examples.controllers.planner_controller Universal adapter that turns any path planner into an engine controller, per robot type.

docs.title: Using a controller
docs.text:
from hivebr.engine import Simulator, load_config
from examples.controllers.potential_field import potential_field_controller

config = load_config("config/default.yaml")
sim = Simulator(config=config, controller=potential_field_controller)
sim.run()

docs.title: Writing one from scratch
docs.text:
import numpy as np

def go_to_goal(robot, world, goal, config, dt, lidar_readings=None):
    if goal is None:
        return {"v": 0.0, "omega": 0.0}

    dx, dy = goal[0] - robot.x, goal[1] - robot.y
    desired = np.arctan2(dy, dx)
    error = np.arctan2(np.sin(desired - robot.theta),
                       np.cos(desired - robot.theta))

    return {"v": min(0.6, np.hypot(dx, dy)), "omega": 2.0 * error}

docs.title: Per-robot dispatch in a fleet
docs.text:
When several B-bots share one controller, the engine calls the controller once per B-bot, passing that B-bot, its own goal and its own LiDAR readings. This is how examples/multi_robot_differential.py reuses a single Kanayama controller across the fleet.

For global, fleet-wide logic (optimization, task allocation), use SwarmController instead — see the OpenLab API.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: This page runs a single B-bot through the low-level engine, which is exactly what examples/single_robot.md does.

docs.title: 1. Configure the world
docs.text:
The engine is driven by a plain dictionary (usually loaded from YAML):

from hivebr.engine import Simulator, load_config

config = load_config("config/default.yaml")
config["robot"]["type"] = "differential"

A minimal configuration looks like this:

window:  { width: 1400, height: 750, panel_width: 300, title: "hivebr" }
world:   { width: 20.0, height: 12.0, grid_size: 1.0, obstacle_radius: 0.4 }
robot:   { type: differential, initial_pose: [2.5, 2.5, 0.0], radius: 0.2,
           max_speed: 3.0, max_omega: 4.0 }
lidar:   { enabled: false, num_rays: 101, range: 12.0, fov_deg: 360 }
theme:   dark

See Configuration for the full reference.

docs.title: 2. Write a controller
docs.text:
A controller is a callable that receives the B-bot, the world, the current goal, the config, the timestep and the LiDAR readings, and returns a command dict.

import numpy as np

def full_controller(robot, world, goal, cfg, dt, lidar_readings=None):
    if goal is None:
        return {"v": 0.0, "omega": 0.0}

    xd, yd, theta_d = goal[0], goal[1], goal[2]
    dx, dy = xd - robot.x, yd - robot.y
    rho = np.hypot(dx, dy)
    if rho < 0.2:
        return {"v": 0.0, "omega": 0.0}

    alpha = np.arctan2(np.sin(np.arctan2(dy, dx) - robot.theta),
                       np.cos(np.arctan2(dy, dx) - robot.theta))
    beta = np.arctan2(np.sin(theta_d - robot.theta - alpha),
                      np.cos(theta_d - robot.theta - alpha))

    v = 0.35 * rho
    w = -1.0 * beta + 1.5 * alpha
    return {"v": v, "omega": w}

The command keys depend on the robot model: - v/omega for differential, differential_firstorder, line_follower, boat - vx/vy for holonomic - speed/steer for ackermann - omega1/omega2/omega3 or vx/vy/omega or v/omega for hexagonal_holonomic

See Robot Models for all kinematic equations.

docs.title: 3. Run
docs.text:
sim = Simulator(config=config, controller=full_controller)
sim.set_using_orientation(True)
sim.set_goal_tolerance(0.2)
sim.set_robot_waypoints(0, [[5, 7, 0.0], [8, 1, 0.0]])
sim.run()

set_robot_waypoints(index, points) sets the route of B-bot index; for a single robot the index is 0.

docs.title: 4. Drive it from the GUI
docs.text:
Once the window is open:

  • Left click adds a waypoint for the selected B-bot.
  • Right click adds an obstacle (a radius dialog appears).
  • Middle drag (or Shift + right drag) pans the view.
  • Mouse wheel zooms.
  • Start / Pause toggles the simulation, Reset restores initial poses.

Full list in User Interface.

Prefer the high-level API?

The same scenario can be expressed with HiveBrAgent and SwarmExperiment. See the OpenLab API and the Decentralized Swarm example.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.8+
  • A desktop environment (the engine opens a Pygame window)

docs.title: From source (recommended)
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/eliasjof/hivebr_simulator.git
cd hivebr_simulator

python -m venv .venv
# Windows
.venv\Scripts\activate
# Linux / macOS
source .venv/bin/activate

pip install -e .

The package uses a src/ layout, so pip install -e . is the easiest way to make import hivebr resolve everywhere. If you prefer not to install, add the source folder to your path:

Windows (PowerShell)Linux / macOS 
$env:PYTHONPATH = "src"

export PYTHONPATH=src

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
hivebr depends on:

Package Version Purpose pygame-ce >=2.5.0 Rendering and event loop pygame_gui >=0.6.9 Interactive control panel numpy >=1.24 Vector math PyYAML >=6.0 Configuration files

Optional extras used by some examples and by occupancy-grid maps:

  • Pillow and scipy (image loading and binary dilation for map inflation).
  • matplotlib (data logger plots).
  • ompl (only for the OMPL planner adapter).

docs.title: Building the documentation
docs.text:
The docs are built with MkDocs Material and mkdocstrings.

pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
mkdocs serve     # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
mkdocs build     # static site into ./site

docs.title: Publishing to GitHub Pages
docs.text:
The .github/workflows/DeployDocs.yml workflow builds the site and pushes it to the gh-pages branch on every push to main.

One-time setup

In Settings → Pages, set the source to the gh-pages branch (root). The site is then available at https://eliasjof.github.io/hivebr_simulator/.

To preview locally:

mkdocs serve

docs.title: Data Logging & Analysis
docs.text:
The engine records the whole fleet every frame while the simulation is running. Each B-bot gets its own time series of pose, commanded velocity and actual velocity, plus a per-frame collision flag. Every collision event (robot–robot, robot–obstacle or robot–grid) is stored separately with its timestamp.

The recorder is sim.logger, an instance of DataLogger created automatically by the Simulator.

docs.title: What gets recorded
docs.text:
Signal Where Notes t, x, y, theta every frame Pose sampled from robot.state(). command every frame Raw controller output (before noise/saturation). real every frame Velocity actually executed (after saturation/kinematics). collision every frame 1 if that B-bot is flagged in collision, else 0. segment every frame New segment whenever new waypoints are added. collision events MultiRobotLog.collision_events {t, kind, robots, ...}.

Command vs. real is exactly what the plot window exposes as separate signals (see Plotting).

docs.title: From the GUI
docs.text: Button Effect Export Log Saves the whole fleet to .pkl (pickle) or .csv, chosen by the dialog's extension. Plot Log Opens the interactive plot window. Reset Logger Discards the recorded log.

docs.title: Programmatically (single Simulator)
docs.text:
sim.run()                         # run the experiment

sim.logger.save("run_01.pkl")     # full log (pickle, recommended)
sim.logger.save_csv("run_01.csv") # per-frame CSV (+ *_collisions.csv)
sim.logger.export("run_02.csv")   # picks pickle/CSV by extension
sim.logger.print_collisions()     # human-readable collision summary
sim.logger.plot()                 # open the interactive plot window

Loading a previously saved run:

from hivebr.engine import DataLogger

log = DataLogger.load("run_01.pkl")   # -> MultiRobotLog
print(log.collision_events)
log.plot_log()

docs.title: Programmatically (decentralized SwarmExperiment)
docs.text:
In decentralized mode the DataLogger lives inside the engine's Simulator, which is created by the navsim2d backend. The experiment exposes it after run():

exp = SwarmExperiment(robots=fleet, backend="navsim2d", config=config)
exp.assign_agent(robot_ids=[0, 1, 2], agent_class=PatrolAgent)
exp.run()

exp.save_log("swarm.pkl")     # .pkl or .csv by extension
exp.print_collisions()        # collisions of the whole experiment
exp.plot_log()                # interactive plot window
# or access the engine directly: exp.simulator.logger

docs.title: Example of a saved log
docs.text:
save_csv("run.csv") writes one row per B-bot per frame, and a companion run_collisions.csv with one row per collision event.

run.csv (per-frame)run_collisions.csv (events) 
robot,robot_type,segment,t,x,y,theta,collision,v,omega,v_real,omega_real,wp_index
0,differential,-1,0.03,2.009,2.0,0.0,1,0.3,0.0,0.3,0.0,0
0,differential,-1,0.06,2.009,2.0,0.0,1,0.3,0.0,0.3,0.0,0
0,differential,-1,0.09,2.009,2.0,0.0,1,0.3,0.0,0.3,0.0,0
0,differential,-1,0.12,2.009,2.0,0.0,1,0.3,0.0,0.3,0.0,0

t,kind,robot_a,robot_b,obstacle_index,obstacle_x,obstacle_y,distance,description
0.03,robot,0,1,,,,0.0,[    0.03s] COLISÃO robô-robô: B-Bot0 <-> B-Bot1 (d=0.000 m)

The pickle (.pkl) keeps the richer object graph and is the format to reload with DataLogger.load:

MultiRobotLog(
    logs=OrderedDict([
        (0, SimLog(robot_type="differential", robot_index=0, label="B-Bot0",
                   frames=[Frame(t=0.03, x=2.009, y=2.0, theta=0.0,
                                 v=0.3, omega=0.0, v_real=0.3, omega_real=0.0,
                                 collision=True, segment=-1), ...])),
        (1, SimLog(...)),
    ]),
    collision_events=[
        {"t": 0.03, "kind": "robot", "robots": [0, 1], "distance": 0.0},
    ],
)

Each collision event carries:

Field Meaning t Simulation time (s) at the rising edge of the collision. kind robot, obstacle or grid. robots The B-bot(s) involved ([i] or [i, j]). obstacle_index / obstacle_xy Obstacle involved (when kind == "obstacle"). distance Surface distance for robot–robot pairs.

DataLogger.print_collisions() renders the same information:

[DataLogger] 2 colisão(ões) registrada(s):
  [    0.03s] COLISÃO robô-robô: B-Bot0 <-> B-Bot1 (d=0.000 m)
  [    1.20s] COLISÃO B-Bot2 com obstáculo #0 em (6.00, 5.00)

docs.title: Plotting the log
docs.text:
The interactive plot window (Tk + Matplotlib) lets you pick B-bots, signals, the subplot grid and whether to overlay B-bots. Velocity signals are available both combined (command vs. actual overlaid on a single axis) and split:

Signal Content Linear velocity (command vs actual) Both linear curves on one axis (solid = command, dashed = actual). Linear velocity (command) Linear command only. Linear velocity (actual) Linear actual only. Angular velocity (command vs actual) Both angular curves on one axis. Angular velocity (command) Angular command only. Angular velocity (actual) Angular actual only.

This makes it easy to see how much of the command the robot actually executed (saturation, first-order lag, collisions, ...).

See the Data Logging API reference for the full surface.

docs.title: Maps & Occupancy Grids
docs.text:
hivebr supports two environment representations at the same time:

  1. Analytic circular obstacles (world.obstacles) — fast, good for prototyping and for adding obstacles interactively.
  2. Image-based occupancy grids (world.grid_map) — pixel maps converted to binary/inflated grids for collision and LiDAR.

docs.title: Occupancy grids
docs.text:
Point the config to an image and give the resolution in metres per pixel:

world:
  map_image: "maze.png"
  resolution: 0.1
  show_inflation: true

Dark pixels (< 128) are treated as occupied. The grid is inflated by the robot radius (plus a 5 cm safety margin) so a point robot never cuts corners.

docs.title: Loading a map at runtime
docs.text:
sim.world.load_map("path/to/map.png", resolution=0.1)
sim.grid_map = sim.world.grid_map

The Load Map button in the GUI does the same and asks for the resolution.

docs.title: Building a grid programmatically
docs.text:
from hivebr.engine import Simulator

grid = my_boolean_array                  # True = occupied
sim.set_map_from_grid(grid, resolution=0.1, name="generated_map.png")

docs.title: Collision and ray casting
docs.text:
occupied = sim.world.grid_map.is_occupied(x, y, use_inflated=True)
distance, hit = sim.world.grid_map.cast_ray(x, y, angle, max_range)

docs.title: Generating benchmark maps
docs.text:
MapGenerator builds classic benchmarking patterns.

from hivebr.engine.map_generator import MapGenerator

grid = MapGenerator.create_grid(type="u")      # "u", "l", "random"
MapGenerator.save(grid, "hivebr/engine/assets/mapa_u.png")

Patterns available:

type Description u U-shaped corridor. l L-shaped corridor. random Randomised maze from a seed.

See MapGenerator API and OccupancyGridMap API.

Optional dependencies

Efficient inflation uses scipy.ndimage.binary_dilation, and image loading uses Pillow. Install them if you rely on occupancy grids.

docs.title: Multi-Robot Fleets
docs.text: hivebr is multi-robot by construction: every B-bot has its own pose, path, waypoint route, LiDAR scan and collision flag. A mono-robot run is just a fleet with N = 1.

docs.title: Declaring a fleet
docs.text:
Add a robots list to the configuration. Each entry overrides the base robot block and may carry a render color.

robots:
  - { id: 0, type: differential, initial_pose: [2.0, 2.0, 0.0], radius: 0.25 }
  - { id: 1, type: differential, initial_pose: [5.0, 5.0, 0.0], radius: 0.25 }
  - { id: 2, type: ackermann,    initial_pose: [18.0, 2.0, 0.0] }

If robots is omitted, the engine builds one B-bot from robot.

docs.title: What the engine exposes
docs.text: Attribute Description sim.robots List of BaseRobot. sim.num_robots Fleet size. sim.waypoint_managers One route per B-bot. sim.robot_lidar_readings One scan per B-bot. sim.collisions One collision flag per B-bot. sim.collision_events Timestamped collision history (robot-robot, obstacle, grid). sim.sim_time Elapsed simulation time (s). sim.selected_robot_index B-bot currently targeted by the GUI. sim.robot, sim.waypoints, sim.lidar_readings, sim.collision Convenience aliases for the selected B-bot.

docs.title: Helpers
docs.text:
sim.set_robot_waypoints(1, [[10, 5, 0.0], [10, 9, 0.0]])   # route for B-bot 1
sim.robot_goal(1)                                          # current waypoint
sim.select_robot(1)                                        # programmatic selection
sim.go_to_recharge_place(id=0, robot_index=2)

docs.title: Deterministic, order-independent stepping
docs.text:
Each timestep the engine:

  1. updates waypoints and LiDAR for every B-bot,
  2. computes all commands from a frozen snapshot of the fleet,
  3. integrates every B-bot simultaneously,
  4. checks static collisions per B-bot,
  5. resolves robot-robot interaction.

Because commands are computed before any B-bot moves, the result does not depend on update order — matching how decentralized agents act on the last received state.

docs.title: Robot-robot interaction
docs.text:
Configure it under interaction:

interaction:
  collision_policy: stop     # "stop" | "resolve" | "none"
  robot_collision: true      # master switch for robot-robot collision checks
  robot_safety_margin: 0.0
  resolve_push: 0.05
  comm_radius: null
  show_robot_links: false
collision_policy Behavior stop Both B-bots of an overlapping pair are flagged and frozen until Reset. resolve Overlaps are relaxed by nudging the pair apart along the normal (resolve_push, capped per step). none Robot-robot collisions are not evaluated at all (no flag, no freeze, no event).

The detection test is distance < r_i + r_j + robot_safety_margin.

docs.title: Disabling robot-robot collision
docs.text:
Set robot_collision: false (or collision_policy: none) to turn the robot-robot check completely off. This is the recommended setup when you want to run the same technique several times in the same arena at the same time — for example several line followers sharing one track and one start point — so the B-bots do not stop when they overlap. Each B-bot keeps evolving independently, which makes the run an apples-to-apples comparison.

config["interaction"] = {
    "collision_policy": "none",
    "robot_collision": False,
}

LiDAR and moving obstacles

Robot-robot collisions are only computed when robot_collision is enabled. While it is enabled, the LiDAR also treats the other B-bots as moving obstacles (circles with each B-bot's radius), so scans include them. When it is disabled, the LiDAR ignores the other B-bots. See Sensors.

docs.title: Communication topology
docs.text:
comm_radius defines visibility for decentralized agents:

  • null → full visibility (every B-bot sees every other).
  • a number → only B-bots within that radius are considered neighbors.

Set show_robot_links: true to draw the resulting communication graph. The same comm_radius is honored by the OpenLab API when building the neighbor list passed to each HiveBrAgent.

docs.title: Per-robot controllers
docs.text:
A single callable controller is invoked once per B-bot with that B-bot's own goal and scan:

sim = Simulator(config=config, controller=full_controller)

For fleet-wide logic, pass a fleet_controller instead:

def fleet_controller(robots, goals, config, dt, lidar_readings):
    # return a list (or {index: command}) with one command per B-bot
    return [{"v": 0.3, "omega": 0.0} for _ in robots]

sim = Simulator(config=config, fleet_controller=fleet_controller)

This is the seam the OpenLab API uses to plug in SwarmController.

docs.title: Interactive fleet control
docs.text: Press 1…9 to select a B-bot; waypoint clicks then target the selected one. The HUD lists every B-bot with its color and collision status. See the Multi-Robot Fleet example.

docs.title: OpenLab API
docs.text:
The hivebr package is a thin, backend-agnostic layer on top of the engine. Its purpose: write your robot logic once and run it either in the local simulator or on the physical arena, in a decentralized or centralized style.

The API never imports Pygame. All rendering lives in hivebr.engine.

docs.title: The dual paradigm
docs.text:
Decentralized (HiveBrAgent) Centralized (SwarmController) Instances One per B-bot (N) Exactly one You receive Your state + neighbors All states Returns A Command (or (v, omega)) {robot_id: Command} Great for Local reactive control, obstacle avoidance, distributed consensus Global planning, optimization (DE, L-SHADE), task allocation Physical backend One ROS 2 node per agent One node publishing per-robot commands

Mono-robot is simply N = 1, with no API change.

docs.title: States and commands
docs.text:
from hivebr import RobotState, Command, FleetState
  • Command(v, omega) — a velocity command.
  • RobotState — an immutable snapshot: id, x, y, theta, v, omega, type, radius, battery, and goal (the current waypoint (x, y) or (x, y, theta), or None).
  • FleetState — t plus {robot_id: RobotState}.

docs.title: Decentralized example
docs.text:
from hivebr import HiveBrAgent, SwarmExperiment

class Patrol(HiveBrAgent):
    def setup(self):
        self.speed = self.params.get("speed", 0.5)

    def loop(self, state, neighbors):
        if state.goal is None:
            return (0.0, 0.0)
        dx = state.goal[0] - state.x
        dy = state.goal[1] - state.y
        theta = state.goal[2] if len(state.goal) > 2 else state.theta
        # ... compute (v, omega) using state and neighbors ...
        return v, omega

exp = SwarmExperiment(robots=3, backend="navsim2d")
exp.assign_agent(robot_ids=[0, 1, 2], agent_class=Patrol, speed=0.6)
exp.assign_route(0, [[5, 2, 0.0], [5, 6, 0.0]])
exp.run()
  • HiveBrAgent.setup() runs once when the experiment builds its agents.
  • loop(state, neighbors) runs every timestep. neighbors is {robot_id: RobotState} filtered by the communication radius.
  • Return a Command, a (v, omega) tuple, or a {"v": …, "omega": …} dict.

docs.title: Centralized example
docs.text:
from hivebr import SwarmController, SwarmExperiment

class GlobalPlanner(SwarmController):
    def loop(self, states):
        return {rid: (0.0, 0.0) for rid in states}

exp = SwarmExperiment(robots=4, backend="navsim2d")
exp.set_controller(GlobalPlanner())
exp.run()

The single controller receives states = {robot_id: RobotState} and returns one command per B-bot, so it can run global optimization over the whole fleet.

docs.title: SwarmExperiment
docs.text:
Member Purpose SwarmExperiment(robots, backend, config, dt, orientation, goal_tolerance, comm_radius) Create an experiment. robots is an int or a list of specs. assign_agent(robot_id=…, robot_ids=[…], agent_class=…, **params) Bind a HiveBrAgent (heterogeneous fleets are supported). set_controller(controller) Bind a SwarmController (centralized mode). assign_route(robot_id, waypoints) Give a B-bot its route. run() Build and run on the selected backend. simulator The engine Simulator created by the navsim2d backend (after run()), giving access to simulator.logger. save_log(path) Save the DataLogger (.pkl or .csv by extension). plot_log() Open the interactive plot window of the recorded log. print_collisions() Print the collision summary of the experiment. reset() / close() Reset agents and backend / tear down.

orientation and goal_tolerance are injected into the engine config, and comm_radius controls neighbor visibility (defaulting to config["interaction"]["comm_radius"]).

docs.title: Saving the log in decentralized mode
docs.text:
In decentralized mode the DataLogger lives inside the engine's Simulator, created by the navsim2d backend, so there is no agent-level logger. After run() the experiment exposes it:

exp.run()

exp.save_log("swarm.pkl")     # .pkl (pickle) or .csv by extension
exp.print_collisions()        # timestamped robot-robot / obstacle / grid events
exp.plot_log()                # interactive plot window

# or reach the logger directly
exp.simulator.logger.save_csv("swarm.csv")

See Data Logging & Analysis for the file formats.

docs.title: How the goal reaches the agent
docs.text: The engine's per-robot waypoint manager supplies the current goal; the bridge copies it into RobotState.goal together with the pose and velocities. Your agent simply reads state.goal.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend Status Description "navsim2d" Available Local Pygame simulation via hivebr.engine. "ros2" Stub Physical arena: one ROS 2 node per agent, or one node for a controller.

Because HiveBrAgent/SwarmController depend only on RobotState/Command, the ROS 2 backend can reuse the exact same user code. See the Bridge & Backends reference.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
• HiveBrAgent, SwarmController, SwarmExperiment
  • RobotState, Command, FleetState
  • Kinematics helpers
  • Bridge & backends

docs.title: Path Planners
docs.text: Planners compute a geometric path from a start pose to a goal. They live in examples/planners and share the BasePlanner interface.

docs.title: BasePlanner
docs.text:
class BasePlanner(ABC):
    def __init__(self, bounds, robot_radius=0.3, seed=None): ...
    def plan(self, start, goal, obstacles, occupancy_map=None) -> (path, DebugData): ...
    @abstractmethod
    def _plan(self, start, goal, obs_list, occupancy_map=None): ...
  • bounds is (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax) in metres.
  • obstacles is world.obstacles (the engine's [x, y, r] arrays).
  • occupancy_map is an optional OccupancyGridMap.
  • plan returns a list of (x, y) from start to goal (or None) and a DebugData object describing the search tree/roadmap for visualization.

Subclasses only implement _plan. Shared collision helpers (_point_free, _segment_free, _in_bounds, _random_sample, _steer, …) are provided by the base class.

docs.title: Available planners
docs.text: Planner Import Class / type A* examples.planners.astar AStarPlanner — grid-based A* on an inflated occupancy grid. RRT examples.planners.planners RRTPlanner — rapidly-exploring random tree. RRT* examples.planners.planners RRTStarPlanner — asymptotically optimal RRT. PRM examples.planners.planners PRMPlanner — probabilistic roadmap. BIT* examples.planners.planners BITStarPlanner — batch informed trees. OMPL examples.planners.ompl_planner OMPLPlanner / OMPLPlannerAdapter — wraps an OMPL planner (RRT, RRTConnect, PRM, BIT*, …). Requires ompl. RRT-Dubins examples.planners.rrtdubins Dubins-path variants for car-like (Ackermann) B-bots.

docs.title: Connecting a planner to the engine
docs.text:
PlannerController turns any planner into an engine controller and draws the path plus debug structure on screen.

from examples.planners.planners import RRTStarPlanner
from examples.controllers.planner_controller import PlannerController
from hivebr.engine import Simulator, load_config

config = load_config("config/default.yaml")
bounds = (0, config["world"]["width"], 0, config["world"]["height"])

planner = RRTStarPlanner(bounds, robot_radius=config["robot"]["radius"], seed=1)
controller = PlannerController(planner)

sim = Simulator(config=config, controller=controller.controller,
                draw_callback=controller.draw_callback)
sim.run()

docs.title: Writing your own planner
docs.text:
from examples.planners.base_planner import BasePlanner, DebugData

class StraightPlanner(BasePlanner):
    def _plan(self, start, goal, obs_list, occupancy_map=None):
        path = [start, goal]
        return path, DebugData()

See also the Controllers page for alternative (reactive) navigation strategies.

docs.title: Robot Models
docs.text:
Every B-bot derives from BaseRobot and exposes a uniform interface:

Member Description robot.position numpy array [x, y]. robot.x, robot.y, robot.theta Scalar pose. robot.state() Dictionary with type, pose, velocity and (for differential) battery. robot.step(command, dt) Advance the kinematics by one timestep. robot.reset() Return to the initial pose. robot.draw(screen, camera) Render the body.

The command you return from a controller depends on the model.

docs.title: Supported Models
docs.text:
type (aliases) Command keys Notes differential (diff, unicycle, nonholonomic) {"v": …, "omega": …} Classic unicycle, with optional battery model. differential_firstorder (firstorder, diff_tau) {"v": …, "omega": …} Adds a first-order lag on the linear speed (tau_v). line_follower (line, linefollower, line_tracker, tcrt5000) {"v": …, "omega": …} Differential kinematics + 2/5/8 analog line sensors (TCRT5000). holonomic (omni, omnidirectional) {"vx": …, "vy": …} Velocity is set directly in world frame. hexagonal_holonomic (hexagonal, hex_holonomic, 3wheel_holonomic) {"omega1": …, "omega2": …, "omega3": …} or {"vx": …, "vy": …} or {"v": …, "omega": …} 3 omni-wheels at 120° (hexagon sides), direct servo control or world-frame velocity. hexagonal_holonomic_line_follower (hex_holonomic_line_follower, 3wheel_holonomic_line_follower) {"v": …, "omega": …} or {"vx": …, "vy": …} or {"omega1": …, "omega2": …, "omega3": …} 3 omni-wheels + TCRT5000 line sensors, PID line following. ackermann (car, racecar) {"speed": …, "steer": …} Bicycle model with front steering. boat {"v": …, "omega": …} Like a differential drive, drawn as a hull. 
# differential
return {"v": 0.5, "omega": 0.1}
# holonomic
return {"vx": 0.5, "vy": 0.0}
# ackermann
return {"speed": 0.5, "steer": 0.2}
# hexagonal holonomic - direct servo control
return {"omega1": 10.0, "omega2": -5.0, "omega3": 3.0}
# hexagonal holonomic - world frame velocity
return {"vx": 0.5, "vy": 0.2, "omega": 0.1}
# hexagonal holonomic line follower - robot frame (v, omega)
return {"v": 0.3, "omega": 0.5}
# hexagonal holonomic line follower - world frame
return {"vx": 0.3, "vy": 0.1, "omega": 0.2}

docs.title: 1. Differential Drive (Unicycle)
docs.text:
Command: {"v": v, "omega": ω}

\[ \begin{aligned} \dot{x} &= v \cos\theta \\ \dot{y} &= v \sin\theta \\ \dot{\theta} &= \omega \end{aligned} \]

Parameters: - max_speed: max linear velocity (m/s) - max_omega: max angular velocity (rad/s) - tau_v: first-order lag time constant (s) — only for differential_firstorder

docs.title: 1b. Differential Drive (First-Order Lag)
docs.text:
Command: {"v": v, "omega": ω}

Same kinematics as differential drive, but with a first-order filter on the linear velocity command:

\[ \begin{aligned} \dot{x} &= v_{\text{act}} \cos\theta \\ \dot{y} &= v_{\text{act}} \sin\theta \\ \dot{\theta} &= \omega \\ \tau_v \dot{v}_{\text{act}} + v_{\text{act}} &= v_{\text{cmd}} \end{aligned} \]

Where: - \(v_{\text{cmd}}\) = commanded linear velocity (from controller) - \(v_{\text{act}}\) = actual linear velocity (after lag) - \(\tau_v\) = time constant (tau_v config parameter)

Parameters (in addition to differential): - tau_v: first-order velocity time constant (s)

docs.title: 2. Holonomic (Omnidirectional)
docs.text:
Command: {"vx": v_x, "vy": v_y} (world frame)

\[ \begin{aligned} \dot{x} &= v_x \\ \dot{y} &= v_y \\ \dot{\theta} &= 0 \quad \text{(independent rotation not directly supported)} \end{aligned} \]

For rotation while translating, use world-frame vx, vy with appropriate values, or use hexagonal_holonomic which supports independent rotation.

docs.title: 3. Hexagonal Holonomic (3-Wheel Omni)
docs.text:
Geometry: 3 omni-wheels at 60°, 180°, 300° (aligned with hexagon flat sides, distance \(L\) from center)

For an omni-wheel at angle \(\phi\) (measured from +x axis), the tangent direction (direction of force/velocity applied to the ground) is perpendicular to the radius vector:

\[ \mathbf{t}(\phi) = \begin{bmatrix} -\sin\phi \\ \cos\phi \end{bmatrix} \]

This gives the wheel tangent vectors:

Wheel Position \(\phi\) Tangent angle \(\phi + 90^\circ\) Tangent vector \(\mathbf{t}\) 1 \(60^\circ\) \(150^\circ\) \(\begin{bmatrix} -\sin 60^\circ \\ \cos 60^\circ \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix}\) 2 \(180^\circ\) \(270^\circ\) \(\begin{bmatrix} -\sin 180^\circ \\ \cos 180^\circ \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}\) 3 \(300^\circ\) \(30^\circ\) \(\begin{bmatrix} -\sin 300^\circ \\ \cos 300^\circ \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix}\)

docs.title: Forward Kinematics
docs.text:
\[ \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \\ \dot{\theta} \end{bmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -r\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & 0 & r\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\[4pt] \frac{r}{2} & -r & \frac{r}{2} \\[4pt] \frac{r}{3L} & \frac{r}{3L} & \frac{r}{3L} \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{J}_f} \begin{bmatrix} \omega_1 \\ \omega_2 \\ \omega_3 \end{bmatrix} \]

Where: - \(r\) = wheel radius (wheel_radius) - \(L\) = distance from robot center to wheel center (radius) - \(\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3\) = wheel angular velocities (rad/s)

docs.title: Inverse Kinematics
docs.text: \[ \begin{bmatrix} \omega_1 \\ \omega_2 \\ \omega_3 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{J}_f^{\dagger} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \\ \dot{\theta} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -\frac{2}{3r} & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3r} & \frac{L}{r} \\[4pt] -\frac{2}{3r} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3r} & \frac{L}{r} \\[4pt] \frac{4}{3r} & 0 & \frac{L}{r} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \\ \dot{\theta} \end{bmatrix} \]

docs.title: Control Modes
docs.text:
Mode Command keys Description Servo (direct) omega1, omega2, omega3 Direct wheel speed control (rad/s) World frame vx, vy, omega World-frame linear + angular velocity Robot frame v, omega Forward speed + angular velocity in robot frame

Parameters: - radius: robot radius (distance center → wheel) \(L\) [m] - wheel_radius: omni wheel radius \(r\) [m] - max_wheel_speed: max wheel angular velocity [rad/s] - max_speed: max robot linear speed [m/s] - max_omega: max robot angular speed [rad/s] - servo_max_speed: max servo speed for control allocation [rad/s]

docs.title: 4. Ackermann (Car-like)
docs.text:
Command: {"speed": v, "steer": \delta}

\[ \begin{aligned} \dot{x} &= v \cos\theta \\ \dot{y} &= v \sin\theta \\ \dot{\theta} &= \frac{v}{L} \tan\delta \end{aligned} \]

Parameters: - max_speed: max linear velocity [m/s] - max_steer: max steering angle [rad] - wheel_base: distance between axles \(L\) [m]

docs.title: 5. Boat
docs.text: Same as differential drive kinematics, rendered as a boat hull.

docs.title: 6. Line Follower (TCRT5000)
docs.text:
Command: {"v": v, "omega": ω}

Uses the same differential-drive kinematics as the differential model:

\[ \begin{aligned} \dot{x} &= v \cos\theta \\ \dot{y} &= v \sin\theta \\ \dot{\theta} &= \omega \end{aligned} \]

Line Sensor Model: The robot carries \(N\) TCRT5000 analog sensors (typically \(N \in \{2, 5, 8\}\)) arranged linearly ahead of the body center. Each sensor returns a normalized reading \(s_i \in [0, 1]\) where: - \(s_i \approx 1\) = over black line - \(s_i \approx 0\) = over white background

The line position error is computed as a weighted centroid: $$ e = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N w_i s_i}{\sum_{i=1}^N s_i} \in [-1, 1] $$

docs.title: 7. Hexagonal Holonomic Line Follower (3-Wheel Omni + TCRT5000)
docs.text:
Command: {"v": v, "omega": ω} (robot frame) or {"vx": v_x, "vy": v_y, "omega": ω} (world frame) or direct servo {"omega1": ω₁, "omega2": ω₂, "omega3": ω₃}

Combines the hexagonal holonomic kinematics (Section 3) with TCRT5000 line sensors.

Kinematics: Same as Hexagonal Holonomic (3 omni-wheels at 60°, 180°, 300°):

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \\ \dot{\theta} \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{J}_f \begin{bmatrix} \omega_1 \\ \omega_2 \\ \omega_3 \end{bmatrix} ,\qquad \mathbf{J}_f = \begin{bmatrix} -r\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & 0 & r\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\[4pt] \frac{r}{2} & -r & \frac{r}{2} \\[4pt] \frac{r}{3L} & \frac{r}{3L} & \frac{r}{3L} \end{bmatrix} \]

Control: Typically uses robot-frame velocity {"v": v, "omega": ω} from a PID line follower: - v = forward speed (clamped to max_speed) - omega = angular velocity from PID on line error (clamped to max_omega)

The controller reads line sensors via robot.read_line_sensors(world.line_map) which provides: - robot.line_error ∈ [-1, 1] (line position error) - robot.sensor_readings array of analog values - robot.line_lost boolean

Parameters (in addition to Hexagonal Holonomic): - num_sensors: 2, 5, or 8 TCRT5000 sensors - line_width: physical line width [m] - sensor_offset: distance from body center to sensor bar [m] - sensor_span: total sensor array width [m] - sensor_aperture: sensing area radius [m] - sensor_noise: Gaussian noise std on readings - line_threshold: threshold for "on line" detection

Lap Timing (same as Line Follower): - lap_detection_radius, min_lap_distance, min_lap_time, lost_timeout

Configuration Example: 

robot:
  type: hexagonal_holonomic_line_follower
  radius: 0.05              # L: center to wheel (m)
  wheel_radius: 0.05        # r: wheel radius (m)
  max_wheel_speed: 20.0
  max_speed: 0.6
  max_omega: 3.5
  servo_max_speed: 20.0
  num_sensors: 5
  line_width: 0.02
  sensor_offset: 0.05
  sensor_aperture: 0.004
  sensor_noise: 0.0
  line_threshold: 0.5
  lap_detection_radius: 0.15
  min_lap_distance: 1.0
  min_lap_time: 1.0
  lost_timeout: 1.0

line_pid:
  base_speed: 0.30
  kp: 4.0
  ki: 0.05
  kd: 0.9
  integral_limit: 1.0

Run Example: 

python examples/run_hexagonal_holonomic_line_follower.py

where \(w_i\) are lateral positions of sensors normalized to \([-1, 1]\).

Parameters (in addition to differential): - num_sensors: number of TCRT5000 sensors (2, 5, or 8) - line_width: physical line width [m] - sensor_offset: distance from body center to sensor bar [m] - sensor_span: total width of sensor array [m] (auto from line_width if omitted) - sensor_aperture: sensing area radius [m] - sensor_noise: Gaussian noise std on readings - line_threshold: threshold for "on line" detection

docs.title: Via YAML Config
docs.text:
robot:
  type: hexagonal_holonomic
  radius: 0.3           # distance center to wheel (m)
  wheel_radius: 0.05    # wheel radius (m)
  max_wheel_speed: 20.0 # max wheel angular speed (rad/s)
  max_speed: 2.0        # max robot linear speed (m/s)
  max_omega: 4.0        # max robot angular speed (rad/s)
  servo_max_speed: 20.0 # max servo speed (rad/s)

docs.title: Programmatically
docs.text: sim = Simulator(config=config, controller=ctrl, type_robot="hexagonal_holonomic")

docs.title: examples/run_hexagonal_holonomic.py
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path
import sys
import math
import numpy as np
from hivebr.engine import Simulator, load_config

def servo_controller(robot, world, goal, config, dt, lidar_readings):
    """Direct servo control using inverse kinematics with control allocation."""
    if goal is None:
        return {"omega1": 0.0, "omega2": 0.0, "omega3": 0.0}

    goal_pos = np.array(goal[:2])
    pos = robot.position
    to_goal = goal_pos - pos
    dist = np.linalg.norm(to_goal)

    tolerance = 0.15
    if dist < tolerance:
        return {"omega1": 0.0, "omega2": 0.0, "omega3": 0.0}

    # World-frame velocity control
    kv = 2.0
    vx_des = kv * to_goal[0]
    vy_des = kv * to_goal[1]

    # Limit linear speed
    speed = math.hypot(vx_des, vy_des)
    if speed > robot.max_speed:
        scale = robot.max_speed / speed
        vx_des *= scale
        vy_des *= scale

    # Angular velocity to align with goal
    goal_angle = math.atan2(to_goal[1], to_goal[0])
    angle_diff = (goal_angle - robot.theta + math.pi) % (2 * math.pi) - math.pi
    kw = 3.0
    omega_des = kw * angle_diff
    omega_des = max(-robot.max_omega, min(robot.max_omega, omega_des))

    # Control allocation: scale until wheels fit within servo limits
    max_servo = robot.servo_max_speed

    for _ in range(5):
        omega1, omega2, omega3 = robot._inverse_kinematics(vx_des, vy_des, omega_des)
        max_wheel = max(abs(omega1), abs(omega2), abs(omega3))
        if max_wheel <= max_servo:
            break
        scale = max_servo / max_wheel
        vx_des *= scale
        vy_des *= scale
        omega_des *= scale

    # Final inverse kinematics
    omega1, omega2, omega3 = robot._inverse_kinematics(vx_des, vy_des, omega_des)

    # Final clamp
    omega1 = max(-max_servo, min(max_servo, omega1))
    omega2 = max(-max_servo, min(max_servo, omega2))
    omega3 = max(-max_servo, min(max_servo, omega3))

    return {"omega1": omega1, "omega2": omega2, "omega3": omega3}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    config = load_config(ROOT / "config" / "hexagonal_holonomic.yaml")
    sim = Simulator(config=config, controller=servo_controller)
    sim.running_simulation = sim.config.get("running_simulation", False)
    sim.run()

docs.text: The sidebar includes sliders to adjust robot parameters at runtime. Enable/disable via config["gui"]["sliders"]:

docs.title: Line Follower (TCRT5000)
docs.text:
LineFollowerRobot keeps differential-drive kinematics but adds analog line sensors.

world:
  line_map_image: config/line_track.png   # black line on white background
  resolution: 0.005                        # metres per pixel

robot:
  type: line_follower
  length: 0.10
  width: 0.10
  line_width: 0.02
  num_sensors: 5            # 2, 5 or 8 TCRT5000
  sensor_offset: 0.05
  sensor_aperture: 0.004
  sensor_noise: 0.0
  line_threshold: 0.5

Read sensors in controller: 

def controller(robot, world, goal, cfg, dt, lidar_readings=None):
    robot.read_line_sensors(world.line_map)
    error = robot.line_error          # -1 (right) .. +1 (left)
    return {"v": 0.3, "omega": 3.0 * error}

See examples/line_follower.py for full PID demo.

Subclass BaseRobot and implement position, reset, state, step, draw, then register in hivebr.engine.robots.create_robot.

from hivebr.engine.robots.base import BaseRobot

class MyRobot(BaseRobot):
    @property
    def position(self):
        return np.array([self.x, self.y])

    def reset(self): ...
    def state(self): ...
    def step(self, command, dt): ...
    def draw(self, screen, camera): ...

See API Reference for class documentation.

docs.title: LiDAR (2D)
docs.text:
The engine provides a configurable 2D LiDAR that ray-casts against both the occupancy grid (DDA algorithm) and the analytic circular obstacles.

lidar:
  enabled: true
  num_rays: 101
  range: 12.0
  fov_deg: 360

docs.title: Reading the scan
docs.text:
Inside a controller, the readings arrive as the last argument:

def controller(robot, world, goal, cfg, dt, lidar_readings=None):
    if lidar_readings:
        angle, distance, hit_point = lidar_readings[0]   # first ray

Each reading is a tuple (angle, distance, hit_point), where angle is in world frame, distance is clamped to range, and hit_point is the world coordinate of the hit.

You can also cast rays on demand:

from hivebr.engine import Simulator, load_config

sim = Simulator(config=load_config("config/default.yaml"))
readings = sim.lidar.cast_rays(sim.robot, sim.world)
# include the other B-bots (with collision enabled) as moving obstacles:
readings = sim.lidar.cast_rays(sim.robot, sim.world, sim.lidar_obstacle_robots())

Other B-bots as moving obstacles

When robot-robot collision is active (interaction.robot_collision: true, the default), the engine feeds the whole fleet to the LiDAR, so every B-bot is seen as a moving circular obstacle with its own radius. If you disable it (robot_collision: false or collision_policy: none), the LiDAR ignores the other B-bots. See Multi-Robot Fleets.

Per-robot scans in a fleet

The engine stores one scan per B-bot in sim.robot_lidar_readings. A per-robot controller receives its own scan; sim.lidar_readings is a convenience alias for the selected B-bot.

docs.title: Line sensors (TCRT5000)
docs.text:
The line_follower B-bot carries an array of analog reflectance sensors (TCRT5000) mounted in a horizontal bar in front of the body. The line is read from a line map: a grayscale image whose dark pixels are the track. The analog reading is 1.0 over the black line and 0.0 over the white background.

values = robot.read_line_sensors(world.line_map)   # array in [0, 1]
error  = robot.line_error          # normalised lateral error in [-1, 1]
offset = robot.line_position       # lateral offset in metres
if robot.line_lost:
    ...                            # no sensor currently sees the line

docs.title: How line_error is computed
docs.text:
1. Sample each sensor. Sensor i sits at a local offset of sensor_offset ahead of the body centre and y_i sideways, with y_i spanning the bar from -sensor_span/2 (the robot's right, -y) to +sensor_span/2 (its left, +y). Each sensor reads the line map over a disk of radius sensor_aperture and returns an analog value value_i in [0, 1].

  2. Weight the sensors from right to left:

weights = linspace(-1, +1, num_sensors)
# index 0 (y = -span/2, right) -> -1 ; last index (y = +span/2, left) -> +1
  1. Normalised, intensity-weighted centroid — the error is the mean of the weights weighted by how strongly each sensor sees the line:
total      = sum(value_i)
line_error = sum(weights_i * value_i) / total      # in [-1, +1]

The sign convention is:

  • line_error > 0 → the line is to the left of the robot (its centre of mass lies under the left sensors);
  • line_error < 0 → the line is to the right;
  • line_error = 0 → the line is centred (or symmetric under the bar);
  • |line_error| = 1 → only the extreme sensor sees the line.

Because a differential B-bot turns left with a positive omega, the natural controller is {"v": base, "omega": kp * line_error}.

  1. Metric offset. Multiply by half the lateral span to get a distance:
line_position = line_error * (sensor_span / 2)      # metres, + = to the left
  1. Lost line. If total ~ 0 (no sensor sees the line) line_lost becomes True and line_error keeps the sign of the last non-zero error, so a controller can keep turning toward where the line was. That last sign is _last_sign, updated on every step where the line is still visible.

Choosing the number of sensors

Use 2, 5 or 8 sensors. With more sensors the weighted centroid resolves the lateral error more finely (smaller quantisation steps). If sensor_span is omitted it is derived from line_width so the line always crosses neighbouring sensors.

docs.title: What you have available
docs.text:
Attribute / method Description robot.read_line_sensors(line_map) Samples the array and updates the fields below; returns the values. robot.sensor_readings numpy array in [0, 1], one entry per sensor (1 = line). robot.line_error Normalised lateral error in [-1, +1]; positive = line to the left. robot.line_position Lateral offset in metres (line_error * sensor_span / 2); positive = left. robot.line_lost True when no sensor sees the line (error keeps the last sign). robot.num_sensors Number of sensors. robot.sensor_offset Forward distance of the bar from the body centre (m). robot.sensor_span Total lateral span of the bar (m). robot.sensor_aperture Radius of the area sampled by each sensor (m). robot.sensor_weights The weights used in the centroid (linspace(-1, 1, N)). robot.sensor_local Local (x, y) of each sensor on the robot body. robot.sensor_world_position(i) World (x, y) of sensor i. robot.line_threshold Reading above which a sensor counts as "on the line".

Configure the array under robot (num_sensors, sensor_offset, sensor_span, sensor_aperture, sensor_noise, line_width). The line map is loaded from world.line_map_image with world.resolution; it is rendered as the arena background and does not participate in collision checks. See Robot Models and examples/line_follower.py.

docs.title: Adding your own sensor
docs.text:
Sensors are plain objects that read from a robot and the world. A minimal sensor that returns the distance to the nearest obstacle:

class RangeSensor:
    def __init__(self, max_range=5.0):
        self.max_range = max_range

    def read(self, robot, world):
        d = world.distance_to_nearest_obstacle(robot.position)
        return min(d, self.max_range)

Wire it into your controller closure, or extend Simulator to store readings alongside robot_lidar_readings.

See the LiDAR API reference.

docs.title: User Interface
docs.text: The engine opens a resizable Pygame window split into a world view (left) and a control panel (right).

docs.title: Mouse and keyboard
docs.text: Input Action Left click (world) Add a waypoint for the selected B-bot. If waypoints.define_orientation is on, a dialog asks for the final heading. Left drag (draw mode) Draw the line-follower track (while Draw Track is active). Right click (world) Add a circular obstacle; a dialog asks for its radius. Middle drag Pan the camera. Shift + right drag Pan the camera (alternative). Mouse wheel Zoom in/out around the cursor. 1 … 9 Select B-bot 0 … 8. The selected B-bot is highlighted in the HUD.

docs.title: Control panel buttons
docs.text: Button Effect Start / Pause Toggle the simulation loop. Reset Restore every B-bot to its initial pose and clear collisions. Clear Path Erase the traced path of every B-bot. Clear Waypoints Remove the routes of all B-bots. Clear Obstacles Remove all circular obstacles. Load Map Load an occupancy-grid image; a dialog asks for the resolution in m/pixel. Draw Track Toggle the line-follower track editor. While on, the simulation pauses and left-drag paints the black line on a white canvas. Apply Track Convert the drawing into a LineTrackMap, install it in the world, save it to world.drawn_line_map_image, and place the B-bot at the start of the stroke (aligned with its tangent). Clear Track Erase the drawing canvas. Toggle LiDAR Enable/disable LiDAR rendering. Toggle Noise Enable/disable the Gaussian velocity noise (noise config section). Toggle Times Show/hide the per-B-bot timing in the HUD (line followers). Toggles config["show_times"]. Toggle Theme Switch between the dark and light palettes. Save Config Write the current world, obstacles and waypoints to config/default.yaml. Center Camera Recenter the view on the world origin. Plot Log Open the interactive plot window (Tk + Matplotlib) to inspect every B-bot: pick robots, signals (trajectory, position/orientation error, linear/angular velocity command vs actual, ...), the subplot grid, and save the figure. Export Log Save the recorded log of the whole fleet to .pkl (pickle) or .csv; collisions go to a companion *_collisions.csv. See Data Logging & Analysis. Reset Logger Discard the recorded log.

docs.text:
The control panel shows parameter sliders that modify the running configuration. Which sliders appear is controlled by config["gui"]["sliders"] (see Configuration).

Slider Config Key Range Applies To Max Speed max_speed 0.2 – 8.0 All except line_follower Max Omega max_omega 0.1 – 6.0 All except line_follower Max Steering max_steer 0.1 – 1.2 Ackermann Grid Size world.grid_size 0.1 – 5.0 All Noise Sigma noise.sigma_v, noise.sigma_omega 0.0 – 1.0 All (enables noise when > 0) Max Servo Speed robot.servo_max_speed 0.5 – 30.0 Hexagonal Holonomic

The sliders update the config dictionary and the robot objects in real time.

docs.title: HUD
docs.text:
The heads-up display shows:

  • A header with run state, fleet size, selected B-bot, FPS, obstacle count and zoom.
  • A detail line for the selected B-bot: type, pose, motion command, waypoint progress, distance to the goal and a [COLLISION] marker. For line followers it also shows laps and timing when show_times is on.
  • One compact line per B-bot, color-coded with its fleet color. A leading * marks a B-bot in collision. For line followers, each line also shows the elapsed time and lap count when Toggle Times is active.
  • A line follower detail row for the selected B-bot: lap count, last lap, average and current lap (or the finish time).

docs.title: Collision indicator
docs.text: When a B-bot is in collision, an explosion sprite is drawn at its position and its HUD line is flagged. With the stop interaction policy the B-bot freezes until Reset. See Multi-Robot Fleets for pairing policies.

This reference is generated automatically from the source code and its docstrings using mkdocstrings. Every page below corresponds to a Python module of the hivebr package.

def get_states(self) -> dict[int, RobotState]:
    if self._sim is None:
        return {}
    robots = getattr(self._sim, "robots", [self._sim.robot])
    states = {}
    for i, robot in enumerate(robots):
        goal = self._sim.robot_goal(i) if hasattr(self._sim, "robot_goal") else None
        states[i] = _state_from_robot(i, robot, goal)
    return states

def create_backend(name: str, experiment) -> Backend:
    key = str(name).lower()
    if key in ("navsim2d", "nav_sim2d", "local", "sim"):
        return NavSim2DBackend(experiment)
    if key in ("ros2", "ros", "arena"):
        return Ros2Backend(experiment)
    raise ValueError(f"Unknown backend: {name!r} (use 'navsim2d' or 'ros2')")

def compute_scale(self):
    scale_x = self.viewport_width / self.world_width
    scale_y = self.viewport_height / self.world_height
    self.base_scale = min(scale_x, scale_y)
    self.scale = self.base_scale * self.zoom

def zoom_at(self, mouse_pos, wheel_y: int):
    old_world = self.screen_to_world(*mouse_pos)
    factor = self.zoom_step if wheel_y > 0 else 1.0 / self.zoom_step
    self.zoom = float(np.clip(self.zoom * factor, self.min_zoom, self.max_zoom))
    self.compute_scale()
    new_world = self.screen_to_world(*mouse_pos)
    self.offset += old_world - new_world

def world_to_screen(self, px: float, py: float):
    ox, oy = self._display_offsets()
    px_cam = px - self.offset[0]
    py_cam = py - self.offset[1]
    sx = int(px_cam * self.scale + ox)
    sy = int(self.viewport_height - (py_cam * self.scale + oy))
    return sx, sy

docs.title: screen_to_world
docs.text:
screen_to_world(sx, sy)
Source code in src/hivebr/engine/camera.py 
def screen_to_world(self, sx: float, sy: float):
    ox, oy = self._display_offsets()
    px = (sx - ox) / self.scale + self.offset[0]
    py = ((self.viewport_height - sy) - oy) / self.scale + self.offset[1]
    return np.array([px, py], dtype=float)

def build_engine_config(self) -> dict:
    cfg = deepcopy(self.config) if self.config is not None else None
    if cfg is None:
        from .engine.simulator import DEFAULT_CONFIG

        cfg = deepcopy(DEFAULT_CONFIG)
    cfg["robots"] = [deepcopy(meta) for meta in self._fleet]
    for index, meta in enumerate(cfg["robots"]):
        meta.setdefault("initial_pose", list(_spread_pose(index)))
        if index in self.routes:
            meta["waypoints"] = [list(wp) for wp in self.routes[index]]

    cfg.setdefault("waypoints", {})
    if self.orientation is not None:
        cfg["waypoints"]["define_orientation"] = bool(self.orientation)
    if self.goal_tolerance is not None:
        cfg["waypoints"]["goal_tolerance"] = float(self.goal_tolerance)
    return cfg

docs.title: data_logger.py
docs.text:
DataLogger genérico para hivebr.engine.

Registra o estado de todos os robôs presentes na arena a cada frame, via draw_callback. Suporta janelas de plot interativas (Tk + Matplotlib) e exportação em pickle e csv.

docs.title: Comportamento de gravação
docs.text:
• Gravação ativa enquanto sim.running_simulation for verdadeiro.
  • Cada robô possui o seu próprio log e a sua própria sequência de segmentos.
  • Um novo segmento é iniciado sempre que novos waypoints são adicionados àquele robô.
  • Cada segmento é identificado pelo campo segment nos frames.
  • Cada frame guarda uma flag collision (por robô). Além disso, toda colisão (robô-robô, obstáculo ou mapa) é registrada em MultiRobotLog.collision_events com o instante t e os participantes; no CSV, essas colisões vão para um arquivo *_collisions.csv.

docs.title: Uso
docs.text:
from hivebr.engine.data_logger import DataLogger

logger = DataLogger()
sim    = Simulator(controller=ctrl)
sim.run()

logger.save("run_01.pkl")      # pickle (recommended)
logger.save_csv("run_01.csv")  # CSV (+ *_collisions.csv)
logger.export("run_01.csv")    # pick format by extension
logger.print_collisions()      # human-readable collision summary
logger.plot()                  # interactive plot window

# Carregar e plotar depois
log = DataLogger.load("run_01.pkl")
log.plot_log()

docs.title: Colisões
docs.text:
Cada frame guarda uma flag collision por robô. Além disso, cada colisão (robô-robô, obstáculo ou mapa) é registrada uma única vez, na borda de subida, em :attr:MultiRobotLog.collision_events no formato

{"t": 0.03, "kind": "robot", "robots": [0, 1], "distance": 0.0}

com kind em {"robot", "obstacle", "grid"}, o instante t e os participantes (índices de robô, obstacle_index/obstacle_xy). No CSV, os eventos vão para um arquivo *_collisions.csv. Ver DataLogger.print_collisions e format_collision_event.

def to_numpy(self) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
    """Converte frames para dicionário de arrays numpy."""
    if not self.frames:
        return {}

    def _get(attr):
        return np.array([getattr(f, attr) for f in self.frames], dtype=float)

    def _get_nullable(attr):
        return np.array(
            [float(v) if (v := getattr(f, attr)) is not None else np.nan
             for f in self.frames], dtype=float,
        )

    result = {
        "t":       _get("t"),
        "x":       _get("x"),
        "y":       _get("y"),
        "theta":   _get("theta"),
        "segment": np.array([f.segment for f in self.frames], dtype=int),
        "collision": np.array([1 if f.collision else 0 for f in self.frames], dtype=int),
    }

    # ação de controle
    for cmd in _ROBOT_CMD_FIELDS.get(self.robot_type, []):
        result[cmd] = _get_nullable(cmd)

    # velocidade real
    for real_key in _ROBOT_REAL_MAP.get(self.robot_type, {}):
        result[real_key] = _get_nullable(real_key)

    # goal
    goals = [f.goal for f in self.frames]
    if any(g is not None for g in goals):
        result["goal_x"] = np.array([g[0] if g is not None else np.nan for g in goals])
        result["goal_y"] = np.array([g[1] if g is not None else np.nan for g in goals])
        if any(len(g) > 2 for g in goals if g is not None):
            result["goal_theta"] = np.array(
                [g[2] if (g is not None and len(g) > 2) else np.nan for g in goals]
            )

    # waypoint atual
    wps = [f.waypoint for f in self.frames]
    if any(w is not None for w in wps):
        result["wp_x"] = np.array([w[0] if w is not None else np.nan for w in wps])
        result["wp_y"] = np.array([w[1] if w is not None else np.nan for w in wps])

    # índice do waypoint
    wp_idx = [f.wp_index for f in self.frames]
    if any(i is not None for i in wp_idx):
        result["wp_index"] = np.array(
            [i if i is not None else -1 for i in wp_idx], dtype=int
        )

    return result

def draw_callback(self, sim, screen):
    if not sim.running_simulation:
        return

    if not self._initialized:
        self._init(sim)

    self._t += sim.dt

    for index in range(len(sim.robots)):
        _, total_wp = self._waypoint_state(sim, index)

        # Novos waypoints -> novo segmento
        if total_wp > self._last_wp_count.get(index, 0):
            self._segment_idx[index] = self._segment_idx.get(index, -1) + 1
            print(f"[DataLogger] B-Bot{index} — segmento "
                  f"{self._segment_idx[index]} iniciado "
                  f"({len(self._logs[index].frames)} frames, "
                  f"{total_wp} waypoints).")

        self._last_wp_count[index] = total_wp
        self._record(sim, index, self._waypoint_manager(sim, index))

def save_csv(self, path: str = "log.csv"):
    """Salva o log completo em CSV (uma linha por robô por frame)."""
    if not self._has_data():
        print("[DataLogger] Nenhum dado para salvar.")
        return

    columns = ["robot", "robot_type", "segment", "t", "x", "y", "theta"]
    arrays: "OrderedDict[int, dict]" = OrderedDict()
    for index in sorted(self._logs):
        arr = self._logs[index].to_numpy()
        arrays[index] = arr
        for key in arr:
            if key not in columns:
                columns.append(key)

    with open(path, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        writer = csv.writer(f)
        writer.writerow(columns)
        for index, arr in arrays.items():
            log = self._logs[index]
            for row in range(len(log.frames)):
                writer.writerow([
                    index if col == "robot"
                    else log.robot_type if col == "robot_type"
                    else arr[col][row] if col in arr
                    else ""
                    for col in columns
                ])

    total = sum(len(l.frames) for l in self._logs.values())
    print(f"[DataLogger] {total} frames / {len(self._logs)} robô(s) -> '{path}'")
    self._write_collisions(self.result().collision_events, path)

def format_collision_event(event: dict) -> str:
    """Formata um evento de colisão em uma linha legível."""
    t = float(event.get("t", 0.0))
    kind = event.get("kind", "?")
    robots = event.get("robots", []) or []
    if kind == "robot":
        pair = " <-> ".join(f"B-Bot{r}" for r in robots)
        dist = event.get("distance")
        dist_txt = f" (d={float(dist):.3f} m)" if dist is not None else ""
        return f"[{t:8.2f}s] COLISÃO robô-robô: {pair}{dist_txt}"
    if kind == "obstacle":
        xy = event.get("obstacle_xy")
        xy_txt = f" em ({float(xy[0]):.2f}, {float(xy[1]):.2f})" if xy else ""
        return (
            f"[{t:8.2f}s] COLISÃO B-Bot{robots[0]} com obstáculo "
            f"#{event.get('obstacle_index')}{xy_txt}"
        )
    if kind == "grid":
        return f"[{t:8.2f}s] COLISÃO B-Bot{robots[0]} com o mapa (inflado)"
    return f"[{t:8.2f}s] COLISÃO {event}"

docs.text:
detect_robot_collisions(robots, safety_margin=0.0)

Return every overlapping pair (i, j, distance) in the fleet.

Uses an O(n^2) sweep, which is fine for the fleet sizes this simulator targets; swap in spatial hashing later if N grows large.

Source code in src/hivebr/engine/interaction.py 
def detect_robot_collisions(robots, safety_margin: float = 0.0) -> list[tuple[int, int, float]]:
    """Return every overlapping pair ``(i, j, distance)`` in the fleet.

    Uses an O(n^2) sweep, which is fine for the fleet sizes this simulator
    targets; swap in spatial hashing later if N grows large.
    """
    pairs: list[tuple[int, int, float]] = []
    n = len(robots)
    for i in range(n):
        pi = robots[i].position
        ri = radius_of(robots[i])
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            d = float(np.linalg.norm(pi - robots[j].position))
            if d < ri + radius_of(robots[j]) + safety_margin:
                pairs.append((i, j, d))
    return pairs

def build_neighbors(robots, comm_radius: float | None = None) -> dict[int, set[int]]:
    """Communication topology: ``{robot_id: {neighbor_ids}}``.

    ``comm_radius=None`` gives full visibility; otherwise only robots within
    the communication radius are considered reachable.
    """
    n = len(robots)
    neighbors: dict[int, set[int]] = {i: set() for i in range(n)}
    for i in range(n):
        pi = robots[i].position
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            d = float(np.linalg.norm(pi - robots[j].position))
            if comm_radius is None or d <= comm_radius:
                neighbors[i].add(j)
                neighbors[j].add(i)
    return neighbors

Separate overlapping robots by nudging them apart along the normal.

Mutates robot positions in place. Called after integration as an optional relaxation to avoid permanently stuck fleets.

Source code in src/hivebr/engine/interaction.py 
def resolve_robot_overlaps(robots, safety_margin: float = 0.0, max_push: float = 0.05) -> None:
    """Separate overlapping robots by nudging them apart along the normal.

    Mutates robot positions in place. Called after integration as an optional
    relaxation to avoid permanently stuck fleets.
    """
    for i, j, d in detect_robot_collisions(robots, safety_margin):
        pi = robots[i].position
        pj = robots[j].position
        normal = pi - pj
        norm = float(np.linalg.norm(normal))
        if norm < 1e-9:
            normal = np.array([1.0, 0.0])
            norm = 1.0
        overlap = radius_of(robots[i]) + radius_of(robots[j]) + safety_margin - d
        push = min(max(overlap * 0.5, 0.0), max_push)
        direction = normal / norm
        robots[i].x += direction[0] * push
        robots[i].y += direction[1] * push
        robots[j].x -= direction[0] * push
        robots[j].y -= direction[1] * push

def apply_limits(
    command: Command,
    max_speed: float,
    max_omega: float,
) -> Command:

        omega=clamp(command.omega, -max_omega, max_omega),
    )

def normalize_command(raw, max_speed: float = None, max_omega: float = None) -> Command:
    """Accept a Command, a (v, omega) tuple, or a mapping and return a Command."""
    if isinstance(raw, Command):
        cmd = raw
    elif isinstance(raw, (tuple, list)):
        cmd = Command(v=float(raw[0]), omega=float(raw[1]))
    elif isinstance(raw, dict):
        cmd = Command(v=float(raw.get("v", 0.0)), omega=float(raw.get("omega", 0.0)))
    else:
        raise TypeError(f"Unsupported command type: {type(raw)!r}")

    if max_speed is not None and max_omega is not None:
        cmd = apply_limits(cmd, max_speed, max_omega)
    return cmd

Source code in src/hivebr/engine/lidar.py 
def ray_circle_intersection(self, ray_origin, ray_dir, obs):
    circle_radius = obs[2]
    circle_center = np.array(obs[:2])
    oc = ray_origin - circle_center
    a = np.dot(ray_dir, ray_dir)
    b = 2.0 * np.dot(oc, ray_dir)
    c = np.dot(oc, oc) - circle_radius ** 2
    disc = b*b - 4*a*c
    if disc < 0:
        return None
    sq = math.sqrt(disc)
    valid = [t for t in [(-b - sq)/(2*a), (-b + sq)/(2*a)] if 0 <= t <= self.range]
    return min(valid) if valid else None

docs.text:
cast_rays(robot, world, other_robots=None)

Faz ray-casting a partir de robot.

other_robots permite tratar os demais B-bots como obstáculos móveis (círculos com o raio do robô). Passe None para ignorá-los.

Source code in src/hivebr/engine/lidar.py 
def cast_rays(self, robot, world, other_robots=None):
    """Faz ray-casting a partir de ``robot``.

    ``other_robots`` permite tratar os demais B-bots como obstáculos
    móveis (círculos com o raio do robô). Passe ``None`` para ignorá-los.
    """
    readings = []
    angles = np.linspace(robot.theta - self.fov/2, robot.theta + self.fov/2, self.num_rays)

    # Check if grid map exists for ray casting
    grid_map = getattr(world, 'grid_map', None)

    # Círculos dos demais robôs (obstáculos móveis).
    robot_circles = []
    if other_robots:
        for other in other_robots:
            if other is robot:
                continue
            robot_circles.append(
                np.array([other.x, other.y, float(other.radius)])
            )

    for angle in angles:
        ray_dir = np.array([math.cos(angle), math.sin(angle)])
        min_d = self.range
        hit = robot.position + ray_dir * self.range

        # 1. Cast against grid map if available
        if grid_map is not None:
            d, h = grid_map.cast_ray(robot.x, robot.y, angle, self.range)
            if d < min_d:
                min_d = d
                hit = h

        # 2. Cast against circular obstacles
        for obs in world.obstacles:
            d = self.ray_circle_intersection(robot.position, ray_dir, obs)
            if d is not None and d < min_d:
                min_d = d
                hit = robot.position + ray_dir * d

        # 3. Cast against the other robots (moving obstacles)
        for circle in robot_circles:
            d = self.ray_circle_intersection(robot.position, ray_dir, circle)
            if d is not None and d < min_d:
                min_d = d
                hit = robot.position + ray_dir * d
        readings.append((angle, min_d, hit))
    return readings

def draw(self, screen, camera, robot, world, other_robots=None):
    if not self.enabled:
        return
    origin = camera.world_to_screen(robot.x, robot.y)
    color = tuple(self.colors["lidar"])

LineTrackMap(image_path, resolution, colors=None)

Mapa de pista de linha (line following).

Carrega uma imagem em tons de cinza onde a linha preta é a trajetória a ser seguida. Diferente do :class:OccupancyGridMap, os pixels escuros são a pista (livre) e os claros são o fundo (fora da linha). A imagem é usada para amostrar sensores analógicos (ex.: TCRT5000), retornando um valor em [0, 1] proporcional à "escuridão" da superfície (1 = linha preta, 0 = fundo branco).

Source code in src/hivebr/engine/line_map.py 
def __init__(self, image_path: str, resolution: float, colors: dict = None):
    self.resolution = float(resolution)
    self.colors = colors if colors is not None else {}

    resolved_path = self._resolve_path(image_path)

    gray = np.array(Image.open(resolved_path).convert("L"), dtype=np.float32)
    self.height, self.width = gray.shape
    self.width_m = self.width * self.resolution
    self.height_m = self.height * self.resolution

    # Inverte verticalmente para alinhar a origem da imagem (topo) com a
    # origem do mundo (canto inferior esquerdo), como no occupancy grid.
    self.darkness = np.flipud(1.0 - gray / 255.0)

    try:
        # A imagem original tem o topo no maior y do mundo (a origem do
        # mundo fica na linha de baixo da imagem), que já coincide com a
        # projeção da câmera (screen_to_world/world_to_screen). Por isso
        # NÃO invertemos aqui — o array `darkness` é que é invertido para a
        # amostragem analógica.
        self.pygame_image = pygame.image.load(resolved_path).convert()
    except Exception as exc:  # pragma: no cover - depends on pygame setup
        print(f"Warning: could not load line map image in Pygame: {exc}")
        self.pygame_image = None

docs.title: sample
docs.text:
sample(x, y, aperture=0.0)

Amostra analógica em (x, y).

aperture é o raio (em metros) da área média em torno do ponto, representando o "campo de visão" do sensor. Fora do mapa retorna 0 (fundo claro / fora da linha).

Source code in src/hivebr/engine/line_map.py 
def sample(self, x: float, y: float, aperture: float = 0.0) -> float:
    """Amostra analógica em ``(x, y)``.

    ``aperture`` é o raio (em metros) da área média em torno do ponto,
    representando o "campo de visão" do sensor. Fora do mapa retorna ``0``
    (fundo claro / fora da linha).
    """
    ix = int(x / self.resolution)
    iy = int(y / self.resolution)

    if ix < 0 or ix >= self.width or iy < 0 or iy >= self.height:
        return 0.0

    radius = int(round(aperture / self.resolution))
    if radius <= 0:
        return float(self.darkness[iy, ix])

    x0 = max(0, ix - radius)
    x1 = min(self.width, ix + radius + 1)
    y0 = max(0, iy - radius)
    y1 = min(self.height, iy + radius + 1)
    return float(self.darkness[y0:y1, x0:x1].mean())

A linha 0 do array corresponde ao topo da imagem (maior y do mundo), como em uma imagem lida do disco.

@classmethod
def from_gray(cls, gray: np.ndarray, resolution: float, colors: dict = None):
    """Cria um mapa de linha a partir de um array ``uint8`` (H, W).

    A linha 0 do array corresponde ao topo da imagem (maior ``y`` do
    mundo), como em uma imagem lida do disco.
    """
    instance = cls.__new__(cls)
    instance.resolution = float(resolution)
    instance.colors = colors if colors is not None else {}

    gray = np.asarray(gray, dtype=np.uint8)
    if gray.ndim == 3:
        gray = gray[:, :, 0]
    instance.height, instance.width = gray.shape
    instance.width_m = instance.width * instance.resolution
    instance.height_m = instance.height * instance.resolution
    instance.darkness = np.flipud(1.0 - gray.astype(np.float32) / 255.0)

    try:
        rgb = np.ascontiguousarray(np.repeat(gray[:, :, None], 3, axis=2))
        instance.pygame_image = pygame.image.frombuffer(
            rgb.tobytes(), (instance.width, instance.height), "RGB"
        ).copy()
    except Exception:  # pragma: no cover - depends on pygame setup
        instance.pygame_image = None

    return instance
